# Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization

###### Abstract

Large language model (LLM) agents have shown promising potential in
coding tasks, and their performance is jointly determined by the policy
model and the harness that mediates their interaction with the
environment. Indeed, harness and policy are mutually reinforcing and
evolving only one component is suboptimal—a harness tuned for one
checkpoint may not target the failure modes of an updated policy, while
policy learning remains limited to the trajectories elicited by a fixed
harness. In light of this, we propose Self-HPO, a recursive
self-improving framework for coding agents that alternates harness and
policy optimization, using the evolving policy as its own harness
proposer. Specifically, in each round, the current policy first analyzes
its own failures and proposes new harness candidates (H-step). The
policy is then updated through reinforcement learning (RL) under the
selected harness (P-step), and hard tasks identified during training
form the next harness search set, keeping harness optimization targeted
to the policy’s evolving failure modes. Across three coding benchmarks,
Self-HPO consistently outperforms harness-only and policy-only
baselines, improving Qwen3.5-35B-A3B’s average resolve rate from 57.8%
to 64.8%, with gains generalizing to out-of-distribution settings.
Further analysis shows that both optimized components retain gains even
when paired with their base counterparts, while their joint gain exceeds
the sum of their individual gains. Self-HPO also improves reliability
(pass@1) and expands the capability frontier (pass@$`k`$) over the base
agent. Additionally, we show that with a stronger external model (e.g.,
Opus 4.8) as the harness proposer, the same framework yields a further
performance boost.

## 1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents have made rapid progress on complex,
multi-step tasks such as software engineering ([Jimenez et al.,
2024](#bib.bib14); [Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib15)), web
navigation ([Zhou et al., 2024](#bib.bib95); [He et al.,
2024](#bib.bib96); [Wei et al., 2025c](#bib.bib97)), and computer
use ([Xie et al., 2024](#bib.bib98); [Agashe et al., 2025](#bib.bib99)).
Such an agent consists of two components: the policy model and its
harness, which is the external scaffold that decides what the model
observes, how its actions are executed, what feedback it receives, and
when an episode terminates ([Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib23); [Shinn et
al., 2023](#bib.bib53); [Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib15); [He et al.,
2024](#bib.bib96); [Lee et al., 2026](#bib.bib16); [Zhang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib18)). Typically, the policy model defines the agent’s
capability boundary, while the harness determines how these capabilities
are elicited, hence the same model may succeed or fail on one problem
depending on its harness ([Le et al., 2026](#bib.bib37); [Zhang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib18)).

There have been two main lines of research on improving such agents.
Harness optimization holds the policy fixed and searches over prompts,
workflows, or agent code ([Hu et al., 2024](#bib.bib42); [Lee et al.,
2026](#bib.bib16); [Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib18)), whereas policy
optimization holds the harness fixed and updates the model from
successful trajectories or verifiable rewards ([Shao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib31); [Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib32); [Wei et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib88)). However, harness-only optimization cannot improve
the underlying model, while policy-only training can learn only from the
trajectories that its fixed harness elicits. Although recent works begin
to optimize both components ([Kim et al., 2026](#bib.bib40); [Chen et
al., 2026a](#bib.bib8)), they rely on an external harness proposer and
face the challenge of a moving optimization target as the policy and its
failure modes evolve, leaving self-driven evolution for coding agents
underexplored.

In this work, we introduce Self-HPO, a framework for recursive
self-improvement driven by the agent’s own policy. As illustrated in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization"),
Self-HPO alternates harness optimization (H-step) with policy
optimization under the optimized harness (P-step). Harness optimization
exposes and compensates for the weaknesses of the current policy, while
policy optimization internalizes the elicited behaviors into the model
and shifts the failures that the next harness should target.
Specifically, in the H-step, the current policy analyzes its failed
trajectories and proposes harness revisions targeting its own failure
modes, and selects the updated harness based on search-set performance
(§[2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 H-step: Failure-Conditioned Harness Search ‣ 2 Self-HPO: Self-Evolving via Harness-Policy Optimization ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")).
In the P-step, the policy is updated using reinforcement learning under
the optimized harness
(§[2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 P-step: Policy Optimization under the Optimized Harness ‣ 2 Self-HPO: Self-Evolving via Harness-Policy Optimization ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")).
In the next H-step, the updated policy serves as the harness proposer,
with hard tasks identified from the preceding P-step as the search set
to keep harness search aligned with the policy’s evolving failure modes.

![Refer to caption](2610.22791v1/teaser_curve.png)

Figure 1: Self-HPO recursively improves the harness and policy using the
agent itself. Left: In each H-step, the current policy proposes an
improved harness, and each P-step then updates the policy through
reinforcement learning with the optimized harness. Right: Average

SWE-Bench Pro along the H- and P-steps. Policy-only and Harness-only

Self-Harness ([Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib18)) baselines.

We instantiate Self-HPO with Qwen3.5-35B-A3B ([Qwen Team,
2026](#bib.bib21)) as the base policy, and mini-SWE-agent ([Yang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib15)) as the seed harness. Across three coding benchmarks,
Self-HPO consistently outperforms policy-only and harness-only
optimization, with the average resolve rate improving at every
optimization step, as demonstrated in
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization").
On SWE-Bench Verified ([Chowdhury et al., 2024](#bib.bib24)), it
improves the base resolve rate from 61.0% to 69.5%, with transferable
gains on the out-of-distribution SWE-Bench Multilingual ([Yang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib25)) and SWE-Bench Pro ([Deng et al., 2025](#bib.bib26)).
Ablations further show that evolving the harness search set with hard
tasks identified during policy learning yields better performance than
reusing a fixed set. We also extend Self-HPO to the external-model setup
where Opus 4.8 is used as an external harness proposer, which further
raises the resolve rate on SWE-Bench Verified to 71.6%. The main
contributions of this work are as follows:

- •
  We propose Self-HPO, a recursive self-improving framework for coding
  agents that alternates harness and policy optimization, where the
  agent uses its own policy as the harness proposer and adapts harness
  search to the policy’s evolving failure modes.
- •
  We demonstrate that Self-HPO consistently outperforms policy-only and
  harness-only baselines across three coding benchmarks, improving the
  average resolve rate from 57.8% to 64.8%, with gains generalizing to
  out-of-distribution settings.
- •
  Our study shows that both optimized components of Self-HPO retain
  gains even when paired with their base counterparts, while their joint
  gain exceeds the sum of their individual gains. We also find that
  Self-HPO not only improves reliability (pass@1) but also expands the
  capability frontier (pass@$`k`$) of the agent.

## 2 Self-HPO: Self-Evolving via Harness-Policy Optimization

![Refer to caption](2610.22791v1/method_overview.png)

Figure 2: Overview of Self-HPO. Top (H-step): The frozen policy analyzes
the agent’s failures on the search set and proposes new harness
candidates. Bottom (P-step): With the updated harness, the policy
evolves through reinforcement learning. The updated policy becomes the
next harness proposer, while tasks never resolved during this P-step
form the next search set.

### 2.1 Problem Setup

Given a software-engineering task $`x`$, a coding agent combines a
policy $`P`$, parameterized by an LLM, with a harness $`H`$, which
controls context, tools, feedback, and termination. The resulting
trajectory $`\tau\sim\pi_{H,P}(\cdot\mid x)`$ is scored by an executable
verifier $`y(x,\tau)\in\{0,1\}`$. We measure a harness–policy pair by
its expected resolve rate on the training data $`\mathcal{D}`$:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
J(H,P)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\,\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi_{H,P}(\cdot\mid x)}\big[y(x,\tau)\big].
``` |  | (1) |

We study the problem of self-improving a coding agent’s own harness and
policy. The harness changes which behaviors the current policy can
reliably express, while a policy update changes the failures that the
next harness should target. As shown in
Figure [2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2 Self-HPO: Self-Evolving via Harness-Policy Optimization ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization"),
each H-step holds the policy fixed while using it to analyze failures
and propose harness revisions, and each P-step then freezes this harness
and updates the policy through reinforcement learning. The updated
policy becomes the next harness proposer, with hard tasks identified
from the training process forming the next search set.

We call this alternating framework Harness-Policy Optimization (HPO) and
implement it in two setups. In the self-improving setup (Self-HPO), the
evolving policy proposes its own harness candidates, so no separate
proposer model is needed. For reference, we also instantiate the same
HPO loop with Opus 4.8 as a fixed external proposer.

1: Seed harness $`H_{0}`$, base policy $`P_{0}`$, training data
$`\mathcal{D}`$, harness search budget $`K`$

2: $`t\leftarrow 0`$, randomly initialize harness search set
$`\mathcal{S}_{t}\subset\mathcal{D}`$

3: while not converged do $`\triangleright`$ Stopping criterion
(§[2](#S2 "2 Self-HPO: Self-Evolving via Harness-Policy Optimization ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization"))

4: /\* H-step: search harness with the current policy as proposer \*/

5:   Score $`v_{0}`$, trajectories
$`\mathcal{T}_{0}\leftarrow\operatorname{Eval}(H_{t},P_{t},\mathcal{S}_{t})`$,
experience $`\mathcal{E}\leftarrow\{(H_{t},\mathcal{T}_{0})\}`$,
$`v_{\mathrm{best}}\leftarrow v_{0}`$, $`H_{t+1}\leftarrow H_{t}`$

6:   for $`k=1,\ldots,K`$ do

7:
   $`H_{t}^{k}\leftarrow\operatorname{ProposeHarness}(H_{t+1},P_{t},\mathcal{E})`$
$`\triangleright`$ Self-proposer
(§[2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 H-step: Failure-Conditioned Harness Search ‣ 2 Self-HPO: Self-Evolving via Harness-Policy Optimization ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization"))

8:
   $`v_{k},\mathcal{T}_{k}\leftarrow\operatorname{Eval}(H_{t}^{k},P_{t},\mathcal{S}_{t})`$,
$`\mathcal{E}\leftarrow\mathcal{E}\cup\{(H_{t}^{k},\mathcal{T}_{k})\}`$

9:    if $`v_{k}>v_{\mathrm{best}}`$ then

10:      $`H_{t+1}\leftarrow H_{t}^{k}`$,
$`v_{\mathrm{best}}\leftarrow v_{k}`$      

11: /\* P-step: train the policy under the updated harness \*/

12:
  $`P_{t+1},\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{RL}}\leftarrow\operatorname{RL}(H_{t+1},P_{t},\mathcal{D})`$

13:
  $`\mathcal{S}_{t+1}\leftarrow\operatorname{SelectHardTasks}(\mathcal{T}_{\mathrm{RL}})`$
$`\triangleright`$ Evolving search set
(§[2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 P-step: Policy Optimization under the Optimized Harness ‣ 2 Self-HPO: Self-Evolving via Harness-Policy Optimization ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization"))

14:   $`t\leftarrow t+1`$

15: return $`H_{t}`$, $`P_{t}`$

Algorithm 1 Self Harness-Policy Optimization (Self-HPO)

A formal description of Self-HPO is presented in
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 2.1 Problem Setup ‣ 2 Self-HPO: Self-Evolving via Harness-Policy Optimization ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization").
Starting from a base policy $`P_{0}`$, a seed harness $`H_{0}`$, and a
random search set $`\mathcal{S}_{0}\subset\mathcal{D}`$, the method
alternates two updates. At round $`t`$ (starting from $`t=0`$), the
H-step keeps $`P_{t}`$ fixed and uses it to propose $`K`$ harness
candidates $`\{H_{t}^{k}\}_{k=1}^{K}`$, retaining the best-scoring
harness on $`\mathcal{S}_{t}`$ as $`H_{t+1}`$. The P-step then freezes
$`H_{t+1}`$ and updates $`P_{t}`$ to $`P_{t+1}`$ on $`\mathcal{D}`$
using reinforcement learning. The resulting training rollouts identify
the next hard-task set $`\mathcal{S}_{t+1}`$ and the loop stops when the
hard-task set stabilizes between rounds.

### 2.2 H-step: Failure-Conditioned Harness Search

#### Self-proposer for harness optimization.

The H-step uses the frozen $`P_{t}`$ as both task solver and harness
proposer. The current pair $`(H_{t},P_{t})`$ first generates
trajectories on $`\mathcal{S}_{t}`$, and the proposer inspects the
current failures and produces targeted revisions to the prompt or
executable runtime logic (see prompt in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Harness Details and Prompt Templates ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")).
Each of the $`K`$ search iterations revises the current best harness,
starting from $`H_{t}`$, using the accumulated experience of all
evaluated harnesses and their trajectories. All candidates are evaluated
on the same search set $`\mathcal{S}_{t}`$.

#### Evolving search set.

The search set remains fixed within an H-step but evolves between
rounds. For initialization, we sample $`\mathcal{S}_{0}`$ uniformly from
$`\mathcal{D}`$. Subsequent search sets consist of hard tasks identified
from the training trajectories generated during the preceding P-step,
where a task is considered hard if it is never resolved in any of its
rollouts in that P-step. The next H-step regenerates trajectories on
those hard tasks with the updated harness–policy pair, producing fresh
failure evidence for proposal. Harness search therefore follows the
failures exposed by the preceding policy update instead of repeatedly
optimizing against the initial tasks.

### 2.3 P-step: Policy Optimization under the Optimized Harness

The P-step improves the policy through reinforcement learning under the
optimized harness $`H_{t+1}`$. Starting from $`P_{t}`$, we collect
on-policy trajectories over $`\mathcal{D}`$ as the policy is updated. An
executable verifier assigns binary outcome rewards, and our default
optimizer combines Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ([Shao et
al., 2024](#bib.bib31)) with Balanced Adaptive Rollout (BAR) from
Orchard ([Peng et al., 2026](#bib.bib17)). BAR adaptively draws
additional trajectories to construct reward-balanced groups, reducing
uninformative zero-variance groups under sparse outcome rewards, and
GRPO then updates the policy using the resulting group-relative
advantages. The tasks that were never resolved during this P-step are
identified as the hard-task set $`\mathcal{S}_{t+1}`$, which will be
passed together with the updated policy $`P_{t+1}`$ to the next H-step.

## 3 Experiments

### 3.1 Experimental Setup

#### Harness, model, and data.

All experiments use Qwen3.5-35B-A3B ([Qwen Team, 2026](#bib.bib21)) as
the base policy and mini-SWE-agent ([Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib23);
[Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib15)) as the seed harness. Following
Orchard ([Peng et al., 2026](#bib.bib17)), we construct a training set
of 2,484 tasks from SWE-rebench ([Badertdinov et al.,
2025](#bib.bib93)), SWE-rebench V2 ([Badertdinov et al.,
2026](#bib.bib20)), and Scale-SWE ([Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib94)),
which is used for both harness search and policy optimization. We
perform two rounds of alternating harness and policy optimization based
on the stopping criterion, with $`K=6`$ harness candidates per H-step
and 50 RL updates per P-step.
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Implementation Details ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")
describes the implementation details.

#### Benchmarks and evaluation metrics.

SWE-Bench Verified (SWE-Verified) contains 500 human-validated GitHub
issues and is our primary benchmark ([Jimenez et al., 2024](#bib.bib14);
[Chowdhury et al., 2024](#bib.bib24)). We further evaluate
out-of-distribution performance on SWE-Bench Multilingual (SWE-Multi;
300 tasks) ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib25)) and the public V2 set of
SWE-Bench Pro (SWE-Pro; 642 tasks) ([Deng et al., 2025](#bib.bib26)),
covering other programming languages and more diverse repository-level
tasks. We report resolve rate, the percentage of tasks whose generated
patches pass the benchmark verifier. Main results are averaged over
three evaluation runs (avg@3) with standard deviations.

#### Baselines.

We compare our method with policy-only and harness-only baselines under
two setups, with the base agent as a reference. In the *self-improving
setup*, RLVR ([Peng et al., 2026](#bib.bib17)) updates the policy under
the seed harness, whereas Self-Harness ([Zhang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib18)) optimizes the harness using the base policy as
proposer without updating its weights. Self-HPO alternates both updates
and uses the current policy to propose harness changes. In the
*external-model setup*, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) learns from
resolved Opus 4.8 trajectories on the same training tasks, while
Meta-Harness ([Lee et al., 2026](#bib.bib16)) uses Opus 4.8 to optimize
the harness with the target policy fixed. HPO combines external harness
proposals with RL policy updates.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|

| Base | ✘ | ✘ | $`61.0{\scriptstyle\,\pm\,0.2}`$ | $`54.2{\scriptstyle\,\pm\,0.3}`$ | $`58.3{\scriptstyle\,\pm\,1.2}`$ | $`57.8{\scriptstyle\,\pm\,0.4}`$ |

|  SFT | ✘ | ✓ | $`65.0{\scriptstyle\,\pm\,1.1}`$ | $`49.6{\scriptstyle\,\pm\,0.8}`$ | $`49.1{\scriptstyle\,\pm\,0.6}`$ | $`54.6{\scriptstyle\,\pm\,0.5}`$ |
| Meta-Harness ([Lee et al., 2026](#bib.bib16)) | ✓ | ✘ | $`69.1{\scriptstyle\,\pm\,1.9}`$ | $`56.5{\scriptstyle\,\pm\,0.9}`$ | $`64.8{\scriptstyle\,\pm\,1.4}`$ | $`63.5{\scriptstyle\,\pm\,0.8}`$ |

### 3.2 Main Results

#### Self-HPO consistently outperforms policy-only and harness-only optimization.

As shown in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Baselines. ‣ 3.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization"),
jointly optimizing the harness and policy achieves the best performance
on all three benchmarks within each setup. Without an external proposer,
Self-HPO reaches $`69.5\%`$ on SWE-Verified, outperforming RLVR and
Self-Harness by $`2.0`$ and $`4.3`$ points, respectively. Its average
score improves from $`57.8\%`$ for Base to $`64.8\%`$, exceeding the
stronger single-component baseline, RLVR, by $`2.9`$ points. The same
pattern holds with external supervision: HPO surpasses Meta-Harness by
$`2.5`$ points on SWE-Verified and $`2.8`$ points on average. These
consistent gains support optimizing the harness and policy together.
Appendix [B](#A2.SS0.SSS0.Px5 "Comparison with frontier models. ‣ Appendix B Additional Evaluation Details ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")
further compares these results with frontier models on SWE-Verified.

#### The gains generalize to out-of-distribution benchmarks.

Although harness search and policy optimization use only tasks from
Python projects, the gains transfer to SWE-Multi, which covers nine
non-Python languages, and SWE-Pro, which spans a broader range of
languages and engineering tasks. Self-HPO achieves $`59.7\%`$ and
$`65.2\%`$, respectively, improving over Base by $`5.5`$ and $`6.9`$
points and over RLVR by $`3.4`$ points on both benchmarks. The benefit
is particularly clear on SWE-Multi, where Self-Harness improves over
Base by only $`0.1`$ point, compared with $`5.5`$ points for Self-HPO.
The same trend holds in the external-model setup, where HPO reaches
$`61.4\%`$ and $`66.0\%`$, outperforming both single-component
baselines. These results show that the benefits of joint harness–policy
optimization extend beyond the Python training domain.

#### Learning from Opus 4.8 through harness optimization is more effective than SFT distillation.

SFT and Meta-Harness represent two different approaches for transferring
knowledge from Opus 4.8: SFT distills generated trajectories into the
model weights, whereas Meta-Harness uses external proposals to optimize
the harness while keeping the model fixed. Meta-Harness outperforms SFT
by $`4.1`$ points on SWE-Verified and $`8.9`$ points on average. The gap
is largest out of domain: SFT falls below Base on both SWE-Multi and
SWE-Pro, while Meta-Harness improves on both. HPO further improves on
Meta-Harness, indicating that policy optimization remains beneficial
when coupled with an optimized harness.

![Refer to caption](2610.22791v1/optimization_trajectories.png)

Figure 3: Optimization trajectories across harness and policy updates.
Resolve rates (%) on SWE-Bench Verified, SWE-Bench Multilingual, and
SWE-Bench Pro are shown on the common
Base–$`H_{1}`$–$`P_{1}`$–$`H_{2}`$–$`P_{2}`$ schedule. Self-HPO
alternates H- and P-steps, whereas Self-Harness and RLVR update only the
harness and policy, respectively. Markers with dashed outlines indicate

#### Alternating harness and policy optimization drives continued agent improvement.

Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Learning from Opus 4.8 through harness optimization is more effective than SFT distillation. ‣ 3.2 Main Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")
traces the optimization trajectories of Self-HPO and the two one-sided
baselines. Self-HPO and Self-Harness begin with the same first H-step,
but their trajectories diverge once Self-HPO updates its policy. Across
all three benchmarks, the second H-step improves the updated Self-HPO
policy, and the following P-step provides a further gain. In contrast,
another harness-only update does not consistently improve performance:
Self-Harness drops from $`55.0\%`$ to $`54.3\%`$ on SWE-Multi. The final
Self-HPO pair surpasses both single-component baselines on every
benchmark, supporting repeated adaptation of the harness to the evolving
policy.
Figure [6](#A2.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Search-frontier curves. ‣ Appendix B Additional Evaluation Details ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")
in the appendix provides a candidate-level view of harness search on
SWE-Verified.

### 3.3 Ablations

We examine the policy-update strategy, search-set construction, and
harness proposer on SWE-Verified.
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.3 Ablations ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")
uses HPO as the reference for ablating the shared H-step–P-step
framework, and replacing its external proposer with the current policy
gives Self-HPO.

| Configuration                 | Resolve rate (%) |
|-------------------------------|------------------|
| HPO                           | 71.6             |
| w/ SFT in P-step              | 67.2 ($`-`$4.4)  |
| w/ RFT in P-step              | 70.5 ($`-`$1.1)  |
| w/ Fixed search set in H-step | 70.1 ($`-`$1.5)  |
| w/ Self-proposer in H-step    | 69.5 ($`-`$2.1)  |

Table 2: Ablation study. Resolve rates reported on SWE-Bench Verified.

#### RL yields stronger policy updates than SFT/RFT.

We replace RL in the P-step with either SFT on trajectories distilled
from Opus 4.8 or rejection-sampling fine-tuning (RFT) on the target
policy’s own successful trajectories. SFT reduces the final resolve rate
from $`71.6\%`$ to $`67.2\%`$, while RFT reaches $`70.5\%`$, trailing RL
by $`1.1`$ points. Even when fine-tuning uses the policy’s own
successful trajectories, it still falls short of RL, supporting RL as
the default P-step.

#### Evolving the search set helps harness optimization keep pace with the policy.

Reusing the initial search set lowers performance from $`71.6\%`$ to
$`70.1\%`$. The evolving set instead directs the next H-step toward hard
tasks from the preceding P-step rollouts. The gain supports refreshing
the search target as the agent improves: failures relevant to an earlier
policy need not remain the most useful targets for its successor.

#### Self-proposal retains strong performance without an external proposer.

Replacing Opus 4.8 with the current target policy yields $`69.5\%`$, a
$`2.1`$-point decrease from HPO. Although external proposals provide an
advantage, Self-HPO still exceeds both self-improving single-component
baselines in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Baselines. ‣ 3.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization").
Therefore, an external model is helpful but not required for our method.

Table 3: Cross-evaluating Self-HPO policies and harnesses on SWE-Bench
Verified. Rows vary the harness and columns vary the policy.

#### Both optimized components retain benefits even when paired with their base counterparts.

Table [3](#S3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 3.4 Analysis ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")
cross-evaluates policies and harnesses. Applying $`H_{2}`$ to the base
policy improves resolve rate from $`61.0\%`$ to $`64.5\%`$, while
deploying $`P_{2}`$ under the seed harness reaches $`64.4\%`$. Combining
$`H_{2}`$ and $`P_{2}`$ reaches $`69.5\%`$, an $`8.5`$-point gain over
Base that exceeds the sum of their individual gains ($`3.5+3.4=6.9`$
points) by $`1.6`$ points. These results show that each component
retains part of the improvement on its own, while combining them gives
the largest gain.

#### Self-HPO improves reliability (pass@1) and expands the capability frontier (pass@$`k`$).

To examine whether the gains persist beyond pass@1,
Figures [4(a)](#S3.F4.sf1 "In Figure 4 ‣ 3.4 Analysis ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")
and [4(b)](#S3.F4.sf2 "In Figure 4 ‣ 3.4 Analysis ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")
compare Base and the final Self-HPO pair using eight attempts per task
on SWE-Verified. As shown in
Figure [4(a)](#S3.F4.sf1 "In Figure 4 ‣ 3.4 Analysis ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization"),
Self-HPO remains above Base for every $`k`$ from 1 to 8, and pass@8
increases from $`80.0\%`$ to $`84.8\%`$, a gain of $`4.8`$ points.
Figure [4(b)](#S3.F4.sf2 "In Figure 4 ‣ 3.4 Analysis ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")
shows pass@1 gains of $`17.2`$ and $`12.9`$ points on Medium and Easy
tasks, where Base sometimes succeeds but remains inconsistent, and a
$`6.1`$-point gain on Hard tasks. At the same time, Self-HPO’s pass@1
decreases by $`2.2`$ points on the Resolved group, showing that
improvement is not uniform across tasks. Together, the gains on Medium
and Easy tasks demonstrate improved reliability, while the gains on Hard
tasks and the higher pass@8 show the expanded capability frontier.

#### Self-HPO reduces zero-success rollout groups during training.

During the final Self-HPO P-step
(Figure [4(c)](#S3.F4.sf3 "In Figure 4 ‣ 3.4 Analysis ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")),
the fraction of zero-success groups, in which no rollout succeeds,
declines to $`6.5\%`$ over the final ten updates, whereas it remains
mostly between $`11\%`$ and $`17\%`$ over the last 50 updates of RLVR.
Under binary outcome rewards, such groups give GRPO no within-group
reward contrast, so reducing them alleviates reward sparsity during
policy optimization.

### 3.5 Case Studies

#### Harness evolution adds targeted controls around the existing agent loop.

Figure [5](#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Self-HPO reduces zero-success rollout groups during training. ‣ 3.4 Analysis ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")
contrasts the seed harness with the harness obtained after HPO’s second
H-step. The optimized harness retains the underlying model-query and
command-execution loop, but intervenes before budget exhaustion and at
submission. First, it warns the model as the step or time limit
approaches and prompts a best-effort submission before the episode ends
with an empty result. Second, a one-time empty-patch guard asks the
model to include newly created files via git add -N. Third, it delays
the first submission that passes the empty-patch guard to prompt a check
of API names and signatures against the repository and tests. Finally, a
fallback uses the sandbox’s Git diff when the submitted patch fails the
apply check. These changes target distinct ways in which useful
repository edits can fail to become a valid submission. They combine
explicit runtime checks, such as detecting an empty patch, with
behavioral guidance, such as requesting an interface check. Harness
optimization can therefore change execution and termination logic, in
addition to prompts.
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Harness Details and Prompt Templates ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")
gives a detailed diff against the seed harness together with the
injected messages, and
Appendix [E](#A5 "Appendix E Case Study: Where the Harness Intervenes ‣ Optimized harness. ‣ Appendix D Harness Details and Prompt Templates ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")
walks through a task on which an evolved harness changes the outcome for
the same policy.

## 4 Related Work

#### Harness optimization for LLM agents.

Harnesses govern an agent’s interaction with tools and
environments ([Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib23); [Yang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib15)). Optimization spans prompts and programs ([Pryzant et
al., 2023](#bib.bib91); [Khattab et al., 2023](#bib.bib50); [Fernando et
al., 2024](#bib.bib51); [Yuksekgonul et al., 2025](#bib.bib90); [Agrawal
et al., 2026](#bib.bib52)), contexts ([Zhang et al., 2026f](#bib.bib41);
[Ye et al., 2026a](#bib.bib56); [Sun et al., 2026](#bib.bib74)), and
workflows ([Hu et al., 2024](#bib.bib42); [Zhang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib43); [Wang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib72); [Gao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib73)). Agents reuse feedback through refinement and
reflection ([Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib54); [Shinn et al.,
2023](#bib.bib53)), skills ([Wang et al., 2023](#bib.bib81)), and
memory ([Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib82); [Wang et al.,
2025c](#bib.bib83)). Program evolution also improves solutions and
agents ([Novikov et al., 2025](#bib.bib77); [Lange et al.,
2026](#bib.bib76); [Zelikman et al., 2024](#bib.bib55); [Zhang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib44); [Zhang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib62)). Recent systems
revise harnesses from execution evidence ([Lee et al.,
2026](#bib.bib16); [Lin et al., 2026a](#bib.bib29); [Zhang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib18); [Park et al., 2026](#bib.bib30); [Wei et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib64); [Xu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib4)), shared
experience ([Weng et al., 2026](#bib.bib71)), demonstrations ([Che et
al., 2026](#bib.bib69); [Jiang et al., 2026](#bib.bib13)), or
self-preferences ([Pan et al., 2026](#bib.bib19)). Other work studies
continual adaptation ([Liu et al., 2026](#bib.bib39); [Xu et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib100)), task selection ([Miyai et al., 2026](#bib.bib67)),
generalization through search controls and modular edits ([Zhang et al.,
2026d](#bib.bib68); [Xia et al., 2026b](#bib.bib9); [Wu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib10)), and fixed-budget evaluation ([Ursekar et al.,
2026](#bib.bib70)). These methods adapt the agent around a fixed
task-solving policy, whereas Self-HPO also updates the policy that the
harness serves.

#### Policy learning and self-improvement.

Iterative training uses filtered reasoning ([Zelikman et al.,
2022](#bib.bib57); [Singh et al., 2024](#bib.bib58); [Yuan et al.,
2023](#bib.bib27)), refreshed preferences ([Chen et al.,
2024](#bib.bib60); [Yuan et al., 2024](#bib.bib59); [Pang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib66)), self-play curricula ([Zhao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib61); [Huang et al., 2026c](#bib.bib47); [Huang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib63)), negative teachers ([Pei et al., 2026](#bib.bib48)),
or evolving environments ([Huang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib49)). Software
engineering agents learn from executable environments ([Pan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib86); [Jain et al., 2025](#bib.bib87); [Yang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib25)), software-evolution supervision ([Wei et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib88)), and self-play code repair ([Wei et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib89); [Choi et al., 2026](#bib.bib80)). Policy improvement
also draws on verifiable-reward RL ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib31);
[Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib32); [Peng et al., 2026](#bib.bib17)),
harness-guided distillation ([Ye et al., 2026b](#bib.bib38)), and
test-time learning during solution search ([Wang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib78); [Yuksekgonul et al., 2026](#bib.bib79)). These
methods train the policy under a fixed harness, whereas in Self-HPO the
harness co-evolves with the policy being trained.

#### Joint harness–policy evolution.

Joint adaptation spans prompts and weights ([Soylu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib2); [Tiwari et al., 2026](#bib.bib3); [Zhang et al.,
2026e](#bib.bib5); [Lu et al., 2026](#bib.bib6)), executable harnesses
and policies ([Hebbar et al., 2026](#bib.bib45); [Karten et al.,
2026](#bib.bib46); [Chen et al., 2026c](#bib.bib33); [Kim et al.,
2026](#bib.bib40); [Luo et al., 2026](#bib.bib35); [Chen et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib36); [Chen et al., 2026a](#bib.bib8)), and policies with
evolving skills or external state ([Xia et al., 2026a](#bib.bib84); [Fu
et al., 2026](#bib.bib85); [He et al., 2026](#bib.bib7); [Ning et al.,
2026](#bib.bib65)), including safety-oriented co-evolution ([Mao et al.,
2026](#bib.bib12)). MetaRSI composes data generation, harness editing,
and model training within a self-improvement loop ([Tan et al.,
2026](#bib.bib1)). Concurrent work traces interventions ([Fan and Huang,
2026](#bib.bib34)), studies transfer and multi-harness training ([Le et
al., 2026](#bib.bib37); [Wei et al., 2026a](#bib.bib11)), and separates
the ability to edit a harness from the ability to benefit from one ([Lin
et al., 2026b](#bib.bib75)). Self-HPO differs from these methods along
two axes. First, the policy trained in the P-step becomes the harness
proposer of the next H-step, whereas WHALE ([Kim et al.,
2026](#bib.bib40)) keeps a frozen external proposer and Evo² ([Xu et
al., 2026a](#bib.bib4)) trains a separate proposer for a frozen solver.
HASE ([Luo et al., 2026](#bib.bib35)) also trains a self-proposing
policy, but places harness edits in the RL action space instead of
alternating harness search with RL. Second, Self-HPO selects the next
harness search set from tasks that remain unsolved during RL, whereas
WHALE, Evo², and HASE search on a fixed task set.
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Conceptual Comparison with Related Methods ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")
gives a more detailed comparison with concurrent work.

## 5 Conclusion

We introduced Self-HPO, a recursive self-improving framework for coding
agents that alternates harness and policy optimization. The evolving
policy proposes its own harness revisions, learns through RL under the
selected harness, and supplies hard tasks for the next round of harness
search. Across three coding benchmarks, Self-HPO consistently
outperforms policy-only and harness-only baselines, improving the
average resolve rate from $`57.8\%`$ to $`64.8\%`$. Analyses further
show that harness and policy improvements are complementary and that
Self-HPO improves reliability (pass@1) and expands the capability
frontier (pass@$`k`$) over the base agent.

## Appendix A Implementation Details

#### Agent implementation.

We use Qwen3.5-35B-A3B ([Qwen Team, 2026](#bib.bib21)) as the backbone
and SGLang ([Zheng et al., 2024](#bib.bib22)) for model serving. RL and
SFT use the slime framework on one node with eight B200 GPUs. The seed
harness follows the mini-SWE-agent interface ([Yang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib15)), through which the model executes bash commands in a
task-specific repository environment.

#### Optimization data.

The initial search set $`\mathcal{S}_{0}`$ consists of 300 tasks
randomly sampled from the training data $`\mathcal{D}`$. For subsequent
H-steps, the search set consists of hard tasks from $`\mathcal{D}`$,
identified using the verified trajectories collected during the
preceding P-step: a task is hard if it is never resolved in any of its
rollouts in that P-step. These task IDs are reused to generate fresh
failure evidence with the updated policy at the next H-step.

#### Harness optimization.

Self-HPO uses the current policy checkpoint as both task solver and
harness proposer. The proposer examines the experience of evaluated
harnesses and their trajectories, including failed trajectories, and
revises the current best harness. HPO instead uses Opus 4.8 to propose
revisions, while retaining the same alternating H-step–P-step structure.
In both configurations, each H-step evaluates $`K=6`$ candidates, each
run once per search task, and the selected harness is held fixed during
the next policy update. The Self-Harness and Meta-Harness baselines use
the same search budget.

#### Policy optimization.

Each P-step initializes from the policy produced by the preceding round
and collects on-policy trajectories under the updated harness. The
executable verifier supplies outcome rewards, and the policy is
optimized with GRPO and Balanced Adaptive Rollout (BAR) ([Shao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib31); [Peng et al., 2026](#bib.bib17)). Let
$`\mathcal{A}(\tau_{i})`$ denote the assistant-generated token positions
in trajectory $`\tau_{i}`$, $`\widehat{A}_{i}`$ its group-relative
advantage, and $`\rho_{i,u}(\theta)`$ the ratio of updated-policy to
rollout-policy token probabilities. The clipped objective is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{P}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{i}\left[\frac{1}{|\mathcal{A}(\tau_{i})|}\sum_{u\in\mathcal{A}(\tau_{i})}\min\left(\rho_{i,u}(\theta)\widehat{A}_{i},\operatorname{clip}(\rho_{i,u}(\theta),1-\varepsilon_{\mathrm{low}},1+\varepsilon_{\mathrm{high}})\widehat{A}_{i}\right)\right],
``` |  | (2) |

where $`\varepsilon_{\mathrm{low}}=0.2`$ and
$`\varepsilon_{\mathrm{high}}=0.28`$ are the clipping thresholds. BAR
generates eight rollouts per task and selects four to form a
reward-balanced group with a success fraction between 0.25 and 0.75.
Sampling continues until 32 groups pass filtering, yielding 128 training
trajectories per batch. Each batch is optimized for one epoch with a
global batch size of 128, corresponding to one optimizer update. We use
Adam with a constant learning rate of $`10^{-6}`$, weight decay 0.01, an
entropy coefficient of $`10^{-4}`$, and no KL penalty. Rollouts use
temperature 0.95 and top-$`p`$ 0.95. RLVR uses the same configuration
under the seed harness, with 50 updates per P-step.

## Appendix B Additional Evaluation Details

#### Evaluation configurations.

All evaluations use a step limit of 250 and temperature and top-$`p`$ of
0.95. Task attempts that fail because of sandbox or API errors are
rerun, and resolve rates are computed over all tasks in each benchmark.

#### SFT configuration.

The SFT baseline in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Baselines. ‣ 3.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")
fine-tunes the base policy on Opus 4.8 trajectories collected on the RL
training tasks, keeping only resolved trajectories. It trains for two
epochs with batch size 64 and a constant learning rate of
$`5\times 10^{-6}`$ after a 10% warmup. In
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 3.3 Ablations ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization"),
SFT instead replaces RL in the P-step of HPO.

#### Search-frontier curves.

![Refer to caption](2610.22791v1/search_frontier.png)

Figure 6: Best-so-far performance during harness evolution on SWE-Bench
Verified. Circles show individual candidate scores. Candidates 1–6 are
shared, while 7–12 belong to the separate Self-Harness and Self-HPO
branches. Vertical increases and stars mark Self-HPO’s two P-steps.
Dashed horizontal lines show Base and final RLVR performance.

Figure [6](#A2.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Search-frontier curves. ‣ Appendix B Additional Evaluation Details ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")
provides a candidate-level view of harness search, complementing the
selected H-step and P-step endpoints in
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ Learning from Opus 4.8 through harness optimization is more effective than SFT distillation. ‣ 3.2 Main Results ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization").
After the shared first H-step reaches $`64.3\%`$, continued harness-only
search improves the best score to $`65.2\%`$. Self-HPO instead updates
the policy to $`67.8\%`$ before resuming search. Its second H-step then
reaches $`68.6\%`$, followed by $`69.5\%`$ after the second policy
update. The separation between the two branches shows the benefit of
policy updates alongside continued harness search.

#### Pass@$`k`$ calculation.

Figure [4](#S3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 3.4 Analysis ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")
compares Base and the final Self-HPO pair with eight attempts per task.
Following [Chen and others (2021)](#bib.bib28), for a task with $`c`$
successes among $`n=8`$ attempts, we compute

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\operatorname{pass@}k=1-\frac{\binom{n-c}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}},\qquad k=1,\ldots,8,
``` |  |

and average over tasks. Pass@1 averages the success frequency, whereas
pass@8 records whether any of the eight attempts succeeds. The shaded
regions show 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.

## Appendix C Conceptual Comparison with Related Methods

Table [5](#A3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ Appendix C Conceptual Comparison with Related Methods ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")
compares Self-HPO with Meta-Harness ([Lee et al., 2026](#bib.bib16)),
Self-Harness ([Zhang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib18)), Task-CoEvolve ([Miyai
et al., 2026](#bib.bib67)), Evo² ([Xu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib4)),
WHALE ([Kim et al., 2026](#bib.bib40)), and HASE ([Luo et al.,
2026](#bib.bib35)) in terms of coverage of the coding domain, how the
policy learns, who proposes harness changes, and how harness-search
tasks are selected.

|  Method |  Coding |  Policy update |  Harness proposer |  Harness search set |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  Meta-Harness |  ✓ |  Frozen |  Frozen external model |  Fixed |
|  Self-Harness |  ✓ |  Frozen |  Frozen self-proposer |  Fixed |
|  Task-CoEvolve |  ✓ |  Frozen |  Frozen external model |  Evolving (high-variance tasks) |
|  Evo² |  ✓ |  Frozen |  Evolving separate proposer |  Fixed |
|  WHALE |  ✘ |  SFT |  Frozen external model |  Fixed |
|  HASE |  ✘ |  RL |  Evolving self-proposer |  Fixed |
|  Self-HPO |  ✓ |  RL |  Evolving self-proposer |  Evolving (hard tasks from RL) |

Table 5: Conceptual comparison of Self-HPO and related methods. Coding
indicates whether the method is evaluated on coding tasks. Policy update
indicates whether the task-solving policy is frozen or updated through
training such as supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or reinforcement learning
(RL). Harness proposer is the model that modifies the harness, which can
be either frozen or updated across rounds. Harness search set denotes
the task set used to collect diagnostic trajectories for harness
optimization. In Self-HPO, the evolving policy itself proposes harness
revisions, and hard tasks identified during training form the next
harness search set, keeping harness optimization targeted to the
policy’s evolving failure modes.

#### The trained solver becomes the next harness proposer.

Self-Harness revises its harness with a fixed policy, WHALE uses a
frozen external proposer alongside policy learning, and Evo² trains a
separate proposer while the task-solving policy stays frozen. Self-HPO
instead reuses the updated task-solving policy as the proposer in the
next round: the H-step holds policy weights fixed, and the P-step
performs RL under the selected harness. HASE also trains a
self-proposing policy, but places task solving and harness editing in a
joint RL action space, with persistent edits reviewed at phase
boundaries.

#### Policy training also determines the next harness-search tasks.

The P-step supplies two inputs to the next H-step: the updated proposer
$`P_{t+1}`$ and a search set $`\mathcal{S}_{t+1}`$ drawn from hard tasks
encountered during RL. Thus, policy learning changes both *who proposes*
and *which tasks guide the search*. Task-CoEvolve also adapts task
selection, but uses outcome variance across candidate harnesses within
search rather than difficulty exposed during policy training. Self-HPO
updates task IDs between H-steps and keeps them fixed within each
H-step.

## Appendix D Harness Details and Prompt Templates

#### Seed harness.

The seed harness $`H_{0}`$ is the mini-SWE-agent ReAct loop ([Yao et
al., 2023](#bib.bib23); [Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib15)): the agent
issues bash tool calls in a task-specific sandbox and ends the episode
by printing the patch after a fixed submission command. Its task prompt
contains the issue description followed by fixed instructions, including
the exact command used to submit the patch.

#### Harness search space.

A candidate harness is a Python class that subclasses the seed agent,
together with its prompt templates. It may override the agent’s step,
for example to inspect the agent’s state, return feedback before
accepting a submission, replace the submitted patch, or intervene at any
step. All repository access goes through the sandbox. The policy and
sampling configuration (temperature and top-$`p`$ of 0.95) are fixed
across candidates.

#### Harness proposer.

Figure [7](#A4.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Harness proposer. ‣ Appendix D Harness Details and Prompt Templates ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")
shows the system prompt of the harness proposer. The proposer runs as a
coding agent with shell access to the parent harness, its trajectories
on the search set, reference fixes for search-set tasks, the outputs of
earlier candidates, and notes that the proposer appends after each
search round.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 7: Harness proposer system prompt (condensed). Values in braces
change between search iterations and rounds. The parent is the current
best harness, and in the first round the search set is the random
$`\mathcal{S}_{0}`$ and the parent starts from the seed harness.
Implementation-specific instructions, such as file paths, the sandbox
interface, and validation scripts, are omitted.

#### Optimized harness.

Figure [5](#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Self-HPO reduces zero-success rollout groups during training. ‣ 3.4 Analysis ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")
shows a condensed view of the harness selected in HPO’s second H-step.
Figure [8](#A4.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Optimized harness. ‣ Appendix D Harness Details and Prompt Templates ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")
shows the same harness as a diff against the seed harness. The optimized
harness keeps the seed prompts unchanged and inherits the seed agent
loop. Its only change is an override of step() that adds four checks.
Three of these checks add a message to the conversation, listed in full
in
Figure [9](#A4.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Optimized harness. ‣ Appendix D Harness Details and Prompt Templates ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization").

`\iow_now:Ne``˝``\iow_now:Ne``˝— seed harness H0: ProgressTrackingAgent.step() (inherited agent loop)``\iow_now:Ne``˝+++ optimized harness: AgentHarness(ProgressTrackingAgent).step()``\iow_now:Ne``˝@@ class AgentHarness(ProgressTrackingAgent) @@``\iow_now:Ne``˝ def step(self):``\iow_now:Ne``˝+ # (1) budget valve: once, shortly before the step or time limit, if nothing was submitted``\iow_now:Ne``˝+ if not self._rescued and not self._submitted_once and (near_step_limit() or near_time_limit()):``\iow_now:Ne``˝+ self._rescued = True``\iow_now:Ne``˝+ self.add_messages(user(RESCUE_TEXT)) # the step then continues as usual``\iow_now:Ne``˝- return self.execute_actions(self.query())``\iow_now:Ne``˝+ try:``\iow_now:Ne``˝+ return self.execute_actions(self.query()) # unchanged seed step``\iow_now:Ne``˝+ except Submitted as e: # the policy issued the submit command``\iow_now:Ne``˝+ self._submitted_once = True``\iow_now:Ne``˝+ sub = e.submission``\iow_now:Ne``˝+ # (2) empty-patch guard: hold an empty submission once``\iow_now:Ne``˝+ if is_empty(sub) and not self._empty_guarded and has_runway():``\iow_now:Ne``˝+ self._empty_guarded = True``\iow_now:Ne``˝+ self.add_messages(user(EMPTY_GUARD_TEXT))``\iow_now:Ne``˝+ return [] # not submitted; the policy continues``\iow_now:Ne``˝+ # (3) contract grounding: hold the first submission that passes the empty guard once``\iow_now:Ne``˝+ if not self._grounded and has_runway():``\iow_now:Ne``˝+ self._grounded = True``\iow_now:Ne``˝+ self.add_messages(user(GROUND_TEXT))``\iow_now:Ne``˝+ return []``\iow_now:Ne``˝+ # (4) patch fallback on the final submission``\iow_now:Ne``˝+ if not is_empty(sub) and not applies_cleanly(sub): # ‘git apply –check‘ on the base commit``\iow_now:Ne``˝+ auth = sandbox("git add -N <untracked files> && git diff")``\iow_now:Ne``˝+ if auth: e.submission = auth # submit the sandbox’s own diff instead``\iow_now:Ne``˝+ raise # accept the submission``\iow_now:Ne``˝`![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)` `

## Appendix E Case Study: Where the Harness Intervenes

To illustrate how an evolved harness changes the outcome for a fixed
policy, we compare two runs of the final Self-HPO policy $`P_{2}`$ on
the SWE-Bench Verified task sphinx-doc\_\_sphinx-9658: one under the
seed harness $`H_{0}`$ and one under the evolved harness $`H_{2}`$. Here
$`H_{2}`$ is the harness from Self-HPO’s second H-step, which differs
from the HPO harness in
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Harness Details and Prompt Templates ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization").
We show the final steps of each run, labeling the task, the agent’s
reasoning, its actions, the resulting observations, and any message
injected by the harness. “$`[\dots]`$” marks omitted content. Purple
notes summarize the key steps, so the example can be followed by reading
them alone.

The two runs reach the same point: the policy has edited the source, the
existing tests pass, and it prepares to finish with a summary of its
changes. Under $`H_{0}`$
(Figure [10](#A5.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ Appendix E Case Study: Where the Harness Intervenes ‣ Optimized harness. ‣ Appendix D Harness Details and Prompt Templates ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")),
this summary becomes the final submission, so no code change is
evaluated. Under $`H_{2}`$
(Figure [11](#A5.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ Appendix E Case Study: Where the Harness Intervenes ‣ Optimized harness. ‣ Appendix D Harness Details and Prompt Templates ‣ Self-Evolving Coding Agents via Harness-Policy Optimization")),
the harness holds the first submission, reports that the submitted patch
contains no files, and returns control to the policy, which writes the
diff, checks the fix, and submits a valid patch. The PR-intent reminder
in this example is a false positive, since its keywords come from
unrelated parts of the issue text.
````
